highlights.title: 'An inspiration to so many' - Olympic runner Mageean dies aged 34
highlights.summary: Portaferry runner Ciara Mageean, who won a European title and twice represented Ireland at the Olympics, dies aged 34.
body: European champion and two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean has died at the age of 34.
Mageean represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics, but was forced to withdraw from the 2024 Paris Games because of an Achilles injury.
Earlier in 2024, she had clinched the first major title of her career when she took 1500m gold at the European Championships in Rome.
Prior to that she had also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning 1500m silver at Birmingham 2022.

highlights.title: Romeo + Juliet at 30: how Baz Luhrmann made teens fall in love with Shakespeare
highlights.summary: The maximalist, heart over head adaptation of the romantic tragedy made stars of its leads and became an English teacher’s most trusted weapon for Bard-averse students. Romeo + Juliet is not the most renowned or beloved of Shakespeare’s plays, but it is perhaps the most foundational.
body: As such, the blatantly youth-aimed film had plenty of detractors in its time. Critics dismissed it as vulgar and garish, but audiences turned out en masse; Romeo + Juliet made over $147m against a $14.5m budget, boosted in part by a period-defining soundtrack with needle drops from The Cardigans, Everclear, Radiohead and Garbage. (And of course, the song from that oft-replayed fish tank scene, Des’ree’s I’m Kissing You, became the ubiquitous soundtrack for couple-shipping montage videos on 2000s YouTube). By the time I first viewed the film in 2009 – like many, in high school English class, as part of my teacher’s bid to get us invested in Shakespeare – it was already considered a classic.

highlights.title: It’s snow time: the best winter activity holidays in Europe for non-skiers
highlights.summary: From husky sledding and chasing the northern lights in Lapland to bear-spotting in Transylvania, here’s our pick of wild and magical snowy breaks in Europe. At Ruka, the first skiers of the year slalomed down the slopes on 2 October.
body: The Narnia-like setting offers just as much action off the runs as on them, and in December the resort launches Ruka Guides, guided adventures from a dedicated activity centre. Spend the morning e-fatbiking through snowy forests (from €90) or cutting a hole in a frozen lake to catch fish (from €89), before learning Arctic survival skills (from €85) or snowshoeing in the evening darkness on the hunt for the northern lights (from €89).

Other, more offbeat diversions include floating in a thermal suit down the freezing Kiveskoski river in meditative silence (from €135), whizzing down an alpine coaster at up to 25mph (from €11.88) and practising your sun salutation in the forest surrounded by grazing reindeer (from €45).

In the depths of winter, the sun sets just a shade after 3.30pm in the Cairngorms national park and doesn’t rise again until about 8.50 the following morning. Those long hours of darkness combined with low levels of light pollution (the area around Tomintoul and Glenlivet is an International Dark Sky Park) makes it the perfect place for stargazing.

highlights.title: Chatbots Are Leading Hikers Astray, With Dangerous Consequences
highlights.summary: Outsourcing planning to AI can lead people to surrender their own critical thinking, which can have potentially deadly results in places like the backcountry.
body: This story originally appeared on High Country News and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

By the time the three hikers called for help from a rocky face on Mount Shasta in Northern California, they’d made a series of bad decisions. They didn’t bring enough food, and they’d overestimated their fitness. Instead of turning back in late afternoon when they hadn’t yet reached the top, they summited at 7:30 pm and had to descend in the dark. Their lack of preparation and poor planning, as they admitted later, came partly from relying on Google’s artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. By morning, they were lost on a gnarly part of the mountain, and one hiker had banged up his knee.

“We get plenty of people who come unprepared or don’t do any research at all. To these guys’ credit, they did try,” said Nick Meyers, US Forest Service program manager of the Mount Shasta Wilderness Climbing and Avalanche Center, which responded to the call. “But I think they kind of turned their brains off.”
points: Outsourcing planning to AI can lead people to surrender their own critical thinking, which can have potentially deadly results in places like the backcountry.

highlights.title: Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims
highlights.summary: Named “Volta-Autodoxer,” the recently uncovered malware uses AI tools to collect troves of data about victims, from login credentials and credit card numbers to Discord sessions and UberEats receipts.
body: New research shared exclusively with Kernel Panic shows that hackers have started adding AI functionality into a new strain of infostealer malware, making it possible for the system to automatically profile victims and quickly surface the highest value targets and their information. Dubbed “Volta-Autodoxer” because of how the malware refers to itself internally, the finding by Cisco Talos researchers sheds light on the ways that commercial LLMs are being used to augment and enhance the capabilities of established types of malware.

“Volta is pretty mature as a stealer. It casts a pretty wide net for what it collects,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos. “It compiles all of those things together, ultimately producing a serialized dossier that it can send to a couple LLM models. It’s asking the model to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim. It’s like a prioritization and analysis function.”

Talos flagged the malware using its new CAIRN framework, built to identify hacking tools that incorporate AI capabilities. Fetterman notes that Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild.

highlights.title: My wife and I are in our late 70s and don’t have any children. Who can help us in our old age? | Annalisa Barbieri
highlights.summary: Getting older and losing your autonomy is even harder without family around. You need to consider both the practical and emotional issues involved. My wife and I are in our late 70s, and have been married for more than 40 years. We didn’t have kids and were rather traumatised after failed IVF.
body: My wife is Asian and has no UK-based family. I do, but they are not close geographically, nor are they people who would be able to give any support if needed. Friends are of a similar age and so have their own issues to deal with. My wife and I have always been a self-reliant unit, and we’re both reasonably healthy, but I’m increasingly aware that there will soon come a time when help is needed.

We should make arrangements for things such as a lasting power of attorney (LPA), but there is nobody we would trust enough and who would be willing to take on that role. As social care for older people slips further into crisis, how can we plan for the inevitable? This must be a problem faced by a significant number of people, but it doesn’t seem to be aired.
I think you’re right: this is a growing problem, and I’d be interested to hear what others have done, since, sadly, I cannot magic up someone for you.

I took your issue to two people: psychoanalytic psychotherapist and CEO of Tavistock Relationships Andrew Balfour, author of Life and Death: Our Relationship With Ageing, Dementia and Other Fates of Time; and estate planning specialist solicitor Gary Rycroft to look at the legal side.

highlights.title: 20 Years Later, The Departed's Best Line Is Still One Of The Greatest Quotes In Gangster Movie History
highlights.summary: In crime cinema, a lethal line of dialogue can carry just as much weight as a loaded gun. Martin Scorsese's Goodfellas hooks audiences with Henry Hill's seductive declaration, “As far back as I can remember, I always wanted to be a gangster,” framing a life of crime as the ultimate aspiration.
body: Yet, for all the memorable quotes the genre has produced, one beats all the rest in sheer gravity. In the opening seconds of Martin Scorsese's The Departed, spoken over documentary footage of 1970s Boston desegregation riots and the unmistakable hum of the Rolling Stones' "Gimme Shelter," Frank Costello (Jack Nicholson) transcends standard tough-guy dialogue with a chilling monologue.
"I don't wanna be a product of my environment. I want my environment to be a product of me."

Two decades later, that phrase still stands apart as truly unforgettable in crime cinema. Costello's introduction is not just a cool piece of gangster posturing, but a cold statement of identity and absolute control, delivered by a sociopath who refuses to accept the world on any terms but his own. His entire worldview defies the natural order.

highlights.title: ‘The term is becoming unrecognisable’: have the experts who believed in a single autism spectrum changed their minds?
highlights.summary: There has been a steep rise in the number of people labelled autistic over the last 20 years. Is that down to greater understanding – or overdiagnosis? The home of 85-year-old Uta Frith does not exactly look like the latest front in the culture wars.
body: “Some of them, I think, are being wrongly influenced by social media to believe that they’re autistic, because it’s a possible way to explain your difficulties,” she tells me. “And then we have a subgroup of people who used to be called neurotic, who have all sorts of mental issues, including anxiety. And a kind of hypersensitivity.”

I have a 20-year-old autistic son, James, who also has learning disabilities – as well as an amazing talent for music – and now goes to a specialist further education college. When he was diagnosed 17 years ago, understanding and awareness of autism seemed to be moving in roughly the right direction. I could never have anticipated the way it has ballooned into a subject of such controversy, which puts me and millions of others in a worldwide community of people who now follow the news with a mixture of bafflement and dread.

highlights.title: Forget Jason Statham, the Best Action Movie of the Last 30 Years Is Back on Netflix
highlights.summary: Harrison Ford spent decades making wildly implausible heroes feel like ordinary guys having a terrible day. An archaeologist outrunning a giant boulder? Sure. A space smuggler taking on an evil empire? Absolutely.
body: Released in 1997, Air Force One stars Ford as President James Marshall, a commander-in-chief who fights back after terrorists hijack his plane. The pitch is essentially “ Die Hard, but John McClane is the president,” and the movie delivers exactly the ridiculous good time that promises. Ford’s charisma somehow makes every punch, speech, and impossible escape feel believable.
Nearly three decades later, Air Force One remains one of the defining action thrillers of the ’90s, and it just landed on Netflix as of Nov. 1. Here’s why it’s still worth watching.

Air Force One was originally released during a very specific moment in American culture. It hit theaters in a stacked summer, competing with Men in Black, The Lost World: Jurassic Park, and Face/Off, and touched down just one year after President Thomas J. Whitmore (Bill Pullman) nobly led humanity to repel an alien invasion in Independence Day. This was during Bill Clinton's second term, not long before the Monica Lewinsky scandal forever changed the public perception of the presidency.

Experiments have shown that students who have mobile phones in class do not perform as well in tests; even having a mobile phone that was off next to you acts as a distractor of your attention.”

Kermode is pretty good at recalling dates. “I’ve got techniques for remembering them, where each month has a particular meaning and/or a colour, and then each day of the month has an object,” she says. “But remembering to actually do something on that birthday – that’s a different thing that I struggle with. highlights.title: A Newly Discovered Trail of Cosmic Debris Illustrates How the End of the Solar System Could Look
highlights.summary: A dying star 1,600 light-years from Earth is surrounded by two rings of gas and dust that astronomers believe are the remnants of the planetary bodies it once hosted.
body: Astronomers at the European Southern Observatory (ESO) have discovered a debris disk around a white dwarf, consisting of the remnants of the solar system that once orbited it. For researchers, these structures could offer a clue as to what the end of our solar system will look like once the sun runs out of fuel.

The white dwarf J1328−1450 is located about 1,600 light-years from Earth. Astronomers were already aware of it thanks to star-mapping catalogs, but new observations taken with ESO’s Very Large Telescope (yes, that’s its real name) revealed that it is surrounded by a disk of debris with an unusual structure: Two distinct rings of gas separated by a gap.

According to the observatory, this disk of material is likely the remnant of the planetary system that once orbited J1328−1450. As it passed through a red giant phase and subsequently became a white dwarf, the star may have destroyed some of its planets and left other rocky bodies exposed to an extreme environment. Some of the released material ended up forming a disk of gas and dust around the dead star.

highlights.title: Meta’s Muse Could Upend All Kinds of Businesses. It Hasn’t Yet
highlights.summary: Companies have spent the past several weeks trying to reassure investors that Muse and other AI agents pose more of an opportunity than a threat.
body: Meta’s Muse was among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks, is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make purchases of more than $200 on average.

Wall Street fears that proactive shopping assistants like Muse will erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. Yet on the earnings calls and in conversations with WIRED, executives across roughly 50 companies—spanning travel, internet providers, food, and self-storage—shrugged off immediate disruption. In fact, many insisted they would mostly benefit from any real widespread adoption of agents.

Food delivery app DoorDash described the number of orders from Muse and other agents as in the “hundreds.” T-Mobile remarked, “We haven’t seen anything of significance” from agents. Hotel chain Hilton was more direct, calling bookings from them “insignificant.” The banking provider Ally Financial characterized activity as “quite low,” while eBay termed it “very, very small.”
points: Companies have spent the past several weeks trying to reassure investors that Muse and other AI agents pose more of an opportunity than a threat.

highlights.title: An AI Agent Injected Drugs Into a Live Mouse’s Brain
highlights.summary: A biotech startup let an agent choose a gene therapy and successfully inject the treatment, offering a startling glimpse of the future of research labs.
body: If you give an AI agent a robotic arm, an injector, and a live mouse, it might just perform brain surgery.

Biotech founder Gabriel Ocana Santero recently did that using an agent to successfully carry out a brain injection procedure on a living mouse. Though it required some extra steps, it offers a glimpse into how AI could eventually become an active participant in laboratory research.

Santero posted about the experiment on social media and tells WIRED he was interested in exploring what happens when AI agents are given direct access to lab equipment, rather than simply being asked to design experiments or analyze results.

“We’ve realized that we need to connect these agents to a lab to get the maximum value from them,” he says. Santero is the CEO and cofounder of Exin Therapeutics, a San Francisco–based startup using AI to analyze brain activity to develop drugs for epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases.

body: "Today?" I whisper hopefully in response to a paragraph of rhetorical questions. "Probably not," snaps back Reality. Especially if I don't get out of bed soon. Still, here in bed I can read the best writing about and not about games from the past week.

At its core, this is about presenting AI as a fait accompli. Every week or so we get a new report making dubious claims about almost every development studio already using AI. The message to developers is "you'll be left behind if you don't use it too"; to players, it's "this is already done and there's no turning back". Consume like good little consumers. Shut up and eat your slop.
A further tonic comes from Merritt K, who writes for Aftermath about the technological improvements rolling through Karaoke.

highlights.title: Let’s Give a Big Hand for Heidi Klum’s 2026 Halloween Costume
highlights.summary: This year, the queen of Halloween transformed herself into a giant replica of her own hand. “I thought it would be funny and bizarre to take something so familiar and twist it.”
body: The star began ideating on the concept about a year ago—even before her 2025 Halloween bash, when she dressed up as Medusa. “Sometimes an idea comes to me very early, and other times I'm still figuring things out closer to Halloween,” says Klum. “I remember trying to explain it to my costume designer, Mike Marino, and he basically told me that he needed to focus on Medusa first! But it stayed in the back of my mind, and I knew I wanted to bring it to life this year.”

As usual, Klum worked her go-to team of special effects artists to bring her delightfully-kooky vision to life. Mike Marino, her right-hand man, led the work with his ProRenFX team. They began by taking a look at Klum’s very own hand for design inspiration. “[Mike] has all of these scans of my body, so he was able to use those to create an exact replica of my hand,” says Klum. “We wanted everything to be as realistic as possible—the anatomy, the veins, the muscles, all the little details that make a hand look like a real hand.”
